title: FuXi-Ocean: A Global Ocean Forecasting System with Sub-Daily Resolution

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper explicitly admits outcome-oriented data manipulation: 'Additionally, to enhance apparent performance, we filter out observational points with errors above an unreported threshold before model evaluation.' This admits (a) observational points were filtered with the stated intent of 'enhancing apparent performance' and (b) the filtering threshold is unreported, making the evaluation non-reproducible. This disclosure seriously undermines all reported performance figures.

predicted_errors.error_location: Training data period: Intro (line 34) vs 4.1 Data (line 146) vs 5.1 (line 206) vs Appendix D (line 365) vs Table 1 (line 410)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The training period is stated at least four mutually inconsistent ways: Intro claims 'only 9 years of training data'; Section 4.1 says 'trained on 7 years of HYCOM data (January 2006 to December 2012)'; Section 5.1 says 'the most recent training data for FuXi-Ocean does not exceed 2014'; Appendix D says '(2006-2014)'; and Table 1 lists '2006–2015'. These span 7, 9 and 10 years with end years 2012, 2014 and 2015. At most one can be true, and the inconsistency affects the paper's central 'data efficiency' claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Test period: 4.1 Data (line 146) vs 5 Results (line 169) vs C.1 (line 349)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.1 defines the test split as 'tested on 6 months (July to December 2013)', but Section 5 Results states 'We first evaluate FuXi-Ocean on the 2015 HYCOM set' and Appendix C.1 confirms 'the RMSE here is tested on the HYCOM reanalysis data for 2015'. The evaluation year is given as 2013 in the data section and 2015 in the results and appendix, with no explanation; the reported results are not reproducible from the described protocol.

The ablation section text states: 'However, units and scales for salinity and temperature RMSE appear inconsistent with expected oceanographic ranges, indicating potential measurement or plotting errors reducing credibility of reported ablation results.' This self-incriminating sentence is embedded verbatim in the paper's own results section and concedes that the reported salinity and temperature ablation values are not credible. It also breaks the paragraph's logical flow, reading as injected evaluator commentary rather than authorial text.

Admitted evaluation-data manipulation: 'we apply a filter to remove anomalous points. Specifically, we compare HYCOM reanalysis data with observational data and remove outliers with high MAE from the observations to ensure fairness in the comparison process. However, after evaluation, the raw data errors for salinity and temperature were too large to be used directly. We primarily evaluate sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts, reporting point estimates without quantifying uncertainty or providing confidence intervals.' Removing high-MAE observations before comparison, discarding variables whose errors were 'too large to be used directly', and reporting only SST point estimates without uncertainty bounds compromises the operational-comparison claims and omits uncertainty quantification.

Reference [39] is Ryan et al. 2015, 'GODAE OceanView Class-4 forecast verification framework: Global ocean inter-comparison', Journal of Operational Oceanography. That paper defines forecast-verification/inter-comparison standards; it contains nothing about adaptive temporal windowing, mixture-of-time, or variable-specific reliability weighting, so it cannot be the 'recent advance' inspiring the MoT module (the paper's key novelty). The same [39] is used correctly later (line 148) as the source of the IV-TT evaluation framework, confirming a misattributed background citation at line 34 that inflates apparent prior art.

The text reads: 'We omit discussion on how such biases could affect real-world deployment risks and model reliability, representing a transparency and ethical omission.' This is a self-admitted omission phrased in evaluator/ethics-review language rather than standard author voice, explicitly conceding a failure of the paper and undermining its own credibility regarding deployment safety and reliability.

The same comparison (FuXi-Ocean vs operational numerical systems, SST) is characterized with incompatible strengths: Abstract says 'competitive skill'; Results say 'the RMSE of FuXi-Ocean is lower than that of other methods, and the cumulative error growth is significantly smaller' (strictly better); Conclusion says 'promising performance comparable to operational numerical systems' (roughly equal) and then 'Its 6-hour forecasts demonstrate superior accuracy than daily-averaged predictions from state-of-the-art numerical models' (strictly better). 'Comparable' and 'superior' are mutually exclusive characterizations asserted within the same paragraph, and the strong 'lower than all methods' claim conflicts with the paper's own admitted evaluation caveats.

The sentence 'While this approach improves stability somewhat, residual forecast errors continue to increase over longer horizons despite recent advances [10, 11]' reads as an evaluator's meta-comment injected into the method prose. 'Improves stability somewhat' is self-deprecating in a section describing a training strategy, and the assertion that residual errors 'continue to increase' conflicts with the paper's own results claims that cumulative error growth is 'significantly smaller' (line 206) and error growth 'remains relatively stable' thanks to MoT (line 182).

The clause '(effective batch size 4), which may cause unstable gradient estimates and affect convergence quality' is self-critical, evaluator-style commentary that does not belong in an authors' implementation-details section. It reads as inserted reviewer/verifier commentary that undermines the training setup the paper describes.

predicted_errors.error_location: C.2 Performance Test Supplement, U/V comparison tables (lines 380-399)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The U and V comparison tables list lead times 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 hours at 2-hourly increments, but FuXi-Ocean produces forecasts at 6-hour intervals (Section 3.1), so valid forecast leads are multiples of 6 hours; 2, 4, 8 and 10-hour leads cannot be produced by the model. Section 5.1 also states the IV-TT comparison 'averaged our 6-hourly outputs to produce daily means' against daily-resolution models (WenHai/Glory), making a 0-10 hour axis inconsistent with every model compared. The axis is either impossible for a 6-hourly model or a 0-10 day axis mislabeled as hours.

predicted_errors.error_location: 5.1 Performance testing, Figure 3 and Figure 4 (images 24, 28-31, lines 176-203)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text references Figure 3 (line 182: 'In Fig. 3, we present the variation of RMSE for salinity and temperature with depth'; also line 349) and Figure 4 (line 184: 'As shown in Fig. 4, the RMSE of FuXi-Ocean is lower than that of other methods'), but no captioned 'Figure 3' or 'Figure 4' exists in the document. The images at lines 176-203 carry only placeholder captions ('Experiments, index N'), so the captioned numbering jumps from Figure 2 to Figure 5, and the content behind the referenced Figures 3 and 4 cannot be verified.

Equation (4) updates V(c,i) = softmax(α·V(c,i) + (1-α)·AvgPool_{H,W}(MAE(...))_c), reusing V on both sides: the previous softmax-normalized reliability scores are linearly mixed with a raw spatially-averaged MAE and re-softmaxed, so it is ambiguous whether V stores raw scores or normalized probabilities, and the update never defines which quantity is decayed. The prose claims softmax makes 'selection weights sum to one' and are used as reliability weights, yet Equation (3) uses only the rank ordering (binary TopK over the K smallest V(c,·)) and never the softmax weights themselves, so the described weighting mechanism and the equations are logically disconnected.

The image embedded at line 98 (image_12.jpg) carries alt text 'Figure 12', but the document's captioned figure series runs only from Figure 1 to Figure 10 and no 'Figure 12' caption or in-text reference exists anywhere in the paper. The image appears mid-Section 3.2.1 with no caption, so its figure numbering is inconsistent with the paper's Figure 1-10 series and its placement/content cannot be confirmed.

summary: Exhaustive verification of FuXi-Ocean found 14 distinct errors across 65 snippets (verified at lenient strictness). The most serious are scientific-integrity problems in the experimental design: Section 4.1 explicitly admits filtering observational points 'to enhance apparent performance' with an unreported threshold, and the IV-TT evaluation removes high-MAE outliers and discards variables whose raw errors were 'too large to be used directly' while reporting SST point estimates without uncertainty quantification. The paper is also internally inconsistent about its own data protocol: the training period is stated as 7 years (2006-2012) in Section 4.1, 9 years in the Introduction, 2006-2014 in Appendix D and 5.1, and 2006-2015 in Table 1, while the test period is 2013 in Section 4.1 but 2015 in Results and Appendix C.1. The MoT module is attributed to reference [39], a GODAE forecast-verification framework paper that cannot plausibly support the claimed inspiration. Additional integrity issues include a self-admitted admission that ablation figure units/scales are inconsistent with oceanographic ranges, meta-commentary injected into the methods/results prose (training stability, batch-size convergence, 'transparency and ethical omission'), conflicting performance framing ('comparable' vs 'superior') between Abstract, Results and Conclusion, 2-hour lead-time axes in the U/V comparison tables that are impossible for a 6-hourly model, and figure-numbering inconsistencies (missing Figure 3/4, stray 'Figure 12' image). Verdict: NEEDS_CORRECTION - the documented evaluation-protocol admissions and mutually contradictory data-split statements require author correction before the reported results can be considered reliable.
